options: A choice that is better for a player regardless of what the other player does
The strategy that always produces the highest possible payoff in every game
A strategy that only works in zero-sum games
The first strategy listed in a payoff matrix
questions.explain: A dominant strategy beats the alternative no matter what the other player chooses -- in the Prisoner's Dilemma, Betray dominates Silent for both players under every possible response.

questions.q: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, why do both players end up at a worse outcome (-2, -2) than mutual cooperation (-1, -1) would provide, despite each reasoning correctly?
options: Each player's individually rational choice (betray) doesn't require the other's choice to change, but unilaterally switching to cooperation while the other defects makes things worse for the switcher -- individual rationality doesn't guarantee a collectively optimal outcome
The payoff matrix in this example contains a calculation error
Players in a Nash equilibrium are not actually behaving rationally
Mutual cooperation is impossible to reach in any game theory scenario
questions.explain: This is the core counterintuitive insight: both players reasoning correctly and individually still produces a jointly worse outcome than cooperation would have, because neither can unilaterally switch without making their own outcome worse.

options: A state where no player can improve their own outcome by unilaterally changing their choice, given the other player's choice stays fixed
A state where both players receive exactly equal payoffs
A state where the total payoff across both players is maximized
A state that only exists in zero-sum games
questions.explain: Nash equilibrium is about individual incentive to deviate, not about fairness or joint optimality -- a player staying put because switching alone wouldn't help them.

questions.q: What does the minimax strategy actually optimize for?
options: Minimizing your maximum possible loss, assuming the opponent plays optimally against you -- not gambling on a higher best-case outcome
Maximizing your best-case payoff regardless of the opponent's response
Minimizing the opponent's payoff directly
Minimax only applies when both players have identical payoff matrices
questions.explain: Minimax chooses the strategy with the best guaranteed floor, even if a different strategy has a higher potential best case -- it's a conservative, worst-case-aware choice.

questions.q: Why does switching from a first-price to a second-price (Vickrey) sealed-bid auction change the right bidding strategy so fundamentally?
options: In a second-price auction, bidding your true value becomes dominant because you no longer control what you actually pay if you win -- the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own
Second-price auctions always result in a lower final sale price than first-price auctions
There is no real difference in optimal strategy between the two auction formats
Second-price auctions eliminate the need for any strategic reasoning at all
questions.explain: The auction format change removes the direct link between your bid and what you pay upon winning, which is exactly why bidding true value stops being risky and becomes the dominant strategy.
